title: The first 60 minutes: triage and containment
body_md:
## The hour starts where the damage is

It is 19:10. Your banking app shows a transfer you never made, your email won’t let you in, and the laptop on the table recently ran a stranger’s remote-support program. Everything feels urgent at once. Nobody standing beside a burning pan begins by working out who left the gas on. They turn off the gas.

“60 minutes” is a rehearsal window, not a deadline or a promise, and no single order of steps suits every case. Begin with the harm that is happening now. An unauthorized bank transfer makes the bank’s fraud line the urgent call; a live email takeover makes account recovery urgent; suspected malware changes which device you trust. Write down the time and what you saw, then act. Working out who the attacker is can wait.

### Three lanes, one for each kind of damage

**Money.** Call the number on your card, or open the bank app yourself rather than through a link in a message. Report the transaction and ask what can be blocked, disputed or recalled. Locking a card may stop the card without stopping a transfer out of the account. Say plainly whether you approved the payment or someone made it without you, because the two are handled differently. Keep the case number and the follow-up steps. Getting the money back is not certain.

**Accounts.** If you are locked out, use the provider’s own recovery page, from a device you have reason to trust. If you are still inside, change the affected password, sign out other sessions where the service allows it, switch on the strongest second factor on offer, and look at recovery contacts, forwarding and connected apps. Email usually comes first, since it often controls the resets for everything else, but not at the cost of a live bank report. A private browser window does nothing for a compromised device.

**Devices and phone number.** If you gave someone remote access, or suspect malware is running, stop using that device for recovery. Disconnect it from the network if that is safe, and work from another device you trust. A work machine, or a case that may need forensic evidence, belongs to your response team: follow their instructions before you wipe or reboot anything. On a personal device, reputable security software and the manufacturer’s support can help, though a clean scan is not proof. If your phone loses service just as odd notices arrive from your carrier, call the carrier on its published support number.

### Before the hour is up

Write down what you know, what you only suspect, and whom you have contacted. Keep alerts and reference numbers somewhere private. Tell an affected colleague or contact just enough to stop them acting on a fraudulent request. What does not fit into the hour carries on; no clock decides when an incident is over.

widget_config.goal: Pick your first containment step from what is actually exposed, then steady money, accounts and devices without treating the hour as a promise.
widget_config.today_action: Write three headings: money, accounts, devices. Under each, put the official contact you would use, and keep the page somewhere you can reach without the affected device.
widget_config.scope: Everyday triage for people in any country. The people and times in the examples are invented. Bank rights, provider controls and workplace forensic procedures differ from place to place.

blocks.title: Money leaving, email locked
blocks.situation: Lina can’t get into her email. While she is trying, the bank app shows a transfer she never approved. She has a second phone that she trusts.
blocks.analysis: She calls the bank on its published number first, because money is leaving now, and only then starts email recovery from the trusted phone. A rule like “email always first” would have held up the one call that can’t wait.

blocks.title: A new-device alert that is just you
blocks.situation: Noor signs into her account on a new tablet, and a new-device alert lands in her inbox a minute later. The account’s activity page lists the tablet and nothing else, and no settings have changed.
blocks.analysis: She notes that the alert matches the tablet and gives the account’s security page a quick look. One genuine sign-in is no reason to freeze every card or wipe the tablet.

blocks.title: Three alarms at 19:10
blocks.setup: An invented evening. At 19:10 your banking app shows a transfer you don’t recognize, and an email says a new device has signed in. Your laptop recently ran a remote-support program you didn’t recognize either. The four decisions below are separate snapshots: each step supplies its own facts, whatever you chose before.

steps.prompt: The transfer is still sitting in the app. What starts the containment?

choices.text: Call the bank on the number from your card or its app, and report the transfer.
choices.consequence: The bank opens its fraud process while the details are fresh.
choices.explanation: Money in motion is the harm happening now. The link in the alert has no part in reporting it.

choices.text: Spend the hour tracing the laptop’s IP address.
choices.explanation: Finding the source can wait. Stopping the damage can’t.

steps.prompt: New snapshot: you are locked out of your email. The laptop ran unknown remote-support software, but you have another device you trust. Where do you recover the account?

choices.text: On the same laptop, in a private window.
choices.consequence: A private window doesn’t remove remote software.
choices.explanation: It changes what the browser remembers, not whether you can trust the device.

choices.text: On the other trusted device, through the provider’s official recovery route.
choices.consequence: Anyone watching the laptop is less likely to see your recovery details.
choices.explanation: Recover from a device you trust, through the provider’s own process and not a link in an alert.

steps.prompt: New snapshot: the laptop ran unknown remote-support software and may still be under someone else’s control. What do you do with it?

choices.text: Disconnect it if that is safe, stop sensitive work on it, find trusted help, and keep workplace evidence as policy requires.
choices.consequence: You cut off access without trusting a scan to call the machine clean.
choices.explanation: A personal laptop and a managed work one are handled differently.

choices.text: Wipe it at once, before writing anything down.
choices.consequence: Evidence, and the records you may need, go with the wipe.
choices.explanation: Containment has to be weighed against keeping evidence.

steps.prompt: New snapshot: an hour later the unfamiliar transfer is still showing, and you may or may not have reached the bank. What next?

choices.text: Assume the risky window has closed.
choices.consequence: An hour is not a verdict. The incident is still open.
choices.explanation: A risky window does not close on a timer. An unreported transfer still needs reporting, and an open case still needs follow-up.

choices.text: Report it now by a known route if you haven’t; if you have, record the case number, open actions and follow-up time.
choices.consequence: You either make the missed report or keep an existing case easy to trace.
choices.explanation: The hour helps you plan. It does not close anything.

blocks.debrief: The order followed the damage: the bank for money in motion, the provider for an account in someone else’s hands, a trusted device for the recovery itself. The hour was only a way to plan. Replay the sequence and take the other choices to see what each one costs.

questions.prompt: A card charge you don’t recognize appears, but your email works normally. What comes first?

choices.text: Report the charge to the card issuer by a known route.
choices.explanation: The issuer can block or dispute it, depending on the type of payment.

choices.text: Change every social media password before speaking to the issuer.
choices.explanation: That delays the financial report and does nothing about the charge.

questions.prompt: You are about to reset a password on a laptop you think is infected. Does a private browser window make that safe?

choices.explanation: Private browsing doesn’t clean a device.

choices.text: No. Use a trusted device, or follow your organization’s response team.
choices.explanation: The device may be compromised, not just the browser’s cookies.

questions.prompt: You were tricked into approving a transfer yourself. How do you describe it to the bank?

choices.text: Say you never authorized it, whatever the facts.
choices.explanation: A false account can send your case down the wrong process.

choices.text: Say exactly what you approved, and ask about recall or dispute options.
choices.explanation: A transfer you were tricked into approving and one made without your say-so can follow different routes.
